patient.name: Tom Whitaker
patient.setting: GP surgery, then the Emergency Department
patient.complaint: Six weeks of bloody diarrhoea with urgency, now worse

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?': blood and tenesmus from the rectum point to UC; non-bloody diarrhoea, weight loss, RIF mass and mouth ulcers point to Crohn's. Severity (Truelove and Witts) and complications (PSC, toxic megacolon) are favourites.

points: Tom, 28: **bloody diarrhoea** for 6 weeks, 5 times a day.
Urgency and **tenesmus**; mucus in the stool.

steps.lead: Tom passes **blood with his stool**: that alone pushes you from IBS towards IBD.
Tom has two risk factors: a **first-degree relative** with UC and recently **stopping smoking**, which can unmask UC.

steps.q: Which type of IBD fits Tom best?
steps.r: Bloody diarrhoea, tenesmus and urgency mean rectal inflammation: **UC** always starts at the rectum. Stopping smoking also fits UC.

steps.lead: Tom's rectal bleeding, urgency and tenesmus are the UC column; Crohn's is non-bloody, with weight loss, RIF mass and mouth ulcers.

steps.title: UC versus Crohn's at the bedside
head: Feature
Ulcerative colitis
Crohn's disease
rows: Fistulae, strictures, perianal disease, B12 deficiency

steps.lead: If Tom is scoped, expect **continuous** inflammation from the anal verge; a patchy, cobbled picture would say Crohn's.

points: Two weeks later he comes to ED: **9 bloody stools** a day.
Crampy pain; feels faint on standing.

visual.title: Bloody stools per day (UC severity)
visual.label: Tom 9
visual.caption: Six or more plus one systemic sign (fever, pulse >90, Hb <105, ESR >30) is **acute severe UC**.

steps.lead: Tom has **9 bloody stools**, a temperature of 38.1°C and a pulse of 104: Truelove and Witts **severe**. Watch for toxic megacolon.
Ask Tom about his joints, eyes, skin and back: IBD brings **extra-intestinal** disease, and PSC can appear years later.

steps.text: In a patient with UC, a cholestatic picture (ALP far higher than ALT) means **primary sclerosing cholangitis** until proven otherwise; confirm on **MRCP**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (colonoscopy with biopsy), plus the safety checks before drugs: TPMT before azathioprine, chest X-ray before infliximab.

steps.title: Tom's bloods in ED
steps.text: Anaemia, high inflammatory markers and a very high calprotectin.

steps.lead: Tom's raised **CRP, ESR** and anaemia show active inflammation; the **faecal calprotectin** separates IBD from IBS.

steps.q: Tom is in a severe flare. Which scope is safest now?
steps.r: Full colonoscopy risks **perforation** in severe colitis; an unprepared flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsies is enough.

steps.lead: Tom's biopsies show crypt abscesses and goblet cell loss: **UC**. Non-caseating granulomas would have meant Crohn's.

steps.title: Biopsy: UC versus Crohn's
head: Finding
UC
Crohn's
rows: Basal plasmacytosis, loss of vascular markings

steps.lead: Tom's abdominal X-ray looks for **toxic megacolon**; MRI small bowel stages Crohn's and MRI pelvis looks for perianal abscess.

visual.title: Colonic diameter on abdominal X-ray
visual.label: Tom 5 cm
visual.caption: Dilatation **above 6 cm** with systemic toxicity defines toxic megacolon; Tom is not there yet.

steps.lead: Before Tom gets azathioprine, ciclosporin or infliximab: **TPMT**, a **chest X-ray** for TB, and **hepatitis B, C and HIV** screening.

steps.text: Low **TPMT** activity means azathioprine builds up and causes **neutropenia**; check it before the first dose.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': topical mesalazine for mild UC, IV hydrocortisone for acute severe UC, then IV ciclosporin or colectomy if no response in 72 hours.

steps.q: Tom has acute severe UC. What is the first treatment?
steps.r: Admit and give **IV corticosteroids**; rescue therapy and surgery come only if he fails to respond.

steps.lead: Tom is admitted for **IV hydrocortisone**, fluids and **LMWH**; the surgeons see him early in case steroids fail.

visual.title: Tom's response to IV hydrocortisone
visual.caption: No real improvement by **72 hours**: time for IV ciclosporin plus surgical review.

points: Day 3: still 8 bloody stools; CRP barely moved.
Started on **IV ciclosporin**; surgical team reviews.
By day 6 he settles to 3 stools a day.

steps.lead: Tom avoids surgery, but if he had not responded, **colectomy** would cure his UC; in Crohn's, surgery is never curative.
Had Tom presented with **mild** UC, topical mesalazine first, then oral 5-ASA. Crohn's induction uses oral prednisolone or budesonide.
For moderate UC the ladder climbs: mesalazine, then oral prednisolone, then calcineurin inhibitors or biologics.

steps.title: UC: from flare to remission
nodes: No response 72 h: IV ciclosporin (or infliximab)
Still failing: colectomy with end ileostomy

steps.lead: Tom goes home on **oral mesalazine**; with 2 or more flares a year he would add **azathioprine**.
Tom's care follows NICE UC guidance, and **Truelove and Witts** decided he needed admission.

steps.text: **Azathioprine interacts with allopurinol** (allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase, which breaks azathioprine down): together they cause marrow suppression.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why UC bleeds while Crohn's fistulates, why mesalazine suits UC, how infliximab works, or the mechanism of diarrhoea.

steps.lead: Tom's disease is **mucosal** and continuous from the rectum; Crohn's goes through the full bowel wall and skips.

steps.title: Depth decides the complications
nodes: Fibrosis and tracking: strictures and fistulae

steps.lead: Tom bleeds because his mucosa is ulcerated; a Crohn's patient forms **fistulae** because the inflammation is transmural.

steps.q: Why does mesalazine work better in Tom than in Crohn's of the terminal ileum?
o: It acts topically on colonic mucosa
It suppresses T cells via calcineurin
steps.r: 5-ASA works **locally on the colon**; small bowel Crohn's gets less benefit.

steps.lead: Tom's colonic disease is exactly where **5-ASA** works.
Crohn's granulomas are a **Th1** response driven by **TNF-alpha**, which is why anti-TNF drugs such as infliximab work.

steps.text: Bloody diarrhoea in UC is from **loss of epithelial integrity**: an ulcerated, inflamed mucosa leaks blood, mucus and fluid.

mcq.q: Which feature best separates IBD from IBS?
mcq.r: Passing blood with stool is the key discriminator.

mcq.q: What is the effect of smoking on UC?
mcq.r: Smoking protects against UC; stopping may trigger it. It is a risk for Crohn's.

mcq.q: Where does Crohn's most commonly occur?
mcq.r: Hence B12 deficiency and RIF mass.

mcq.q: Which is part of Truelove and Witts' severe UC?
o: ≥6 bloody stools a day plus pulse >90
mcq.r: Six bloody stools plus one systemic marker.

mcq.q: Which liver disease is linked to UC?
What is the gold standard test for IBD?
What must be checked before azathioprine?

mcq.r: Crypt abscesses and goblet cell loss are UC.

mcq.q: First-line treatment for acute severe UC?
mcq.r: Ciclosporin if no response in 48–72 hours.

mcq.q: Why does Crohn's form fistulae but UC rarely does?
mcq.r: Full-thickness inflammation tracks to other organs.

prompts.q: Who gets IBD? Give the risk factors and how smoking affects each type.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: smoking cuts both ways.

points.p: First-degree relative with UC: seven-fold risk
Crohn's presents before 40, second smaller peak later
Smoking: risk for Crohn's, protective for UC

prompts.q: How does ulcerative colitis present, and where is it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: rectal symptoms plus blood.

points.p: Starts at rectum, continuous, colon only

prompts.q: How does Crohn's disease present, and where is it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: mouth to anus, mass in the RIF.

points.p: Terminal ileum most often, anywhere mouth to anus
Aphthous mouth ulcers and perianal disease (tags, fissures, fistulae)

prompts.q: What are the Truelove and Witts' criteria for severe UC?

points.p: 6 or more bloody stools a day

prompts.q: Define toxic megacolon and name the hepatobiliary complications of UC.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: over 6 cm and toxic.

points.p: Plus 3 of: temp >38, HR >120, neutrophilia, anaemia; and one of dehydration, confusion, electrolyte disturbance, hypotension
Primary sclerosing cholangitis: ALP raised more than ALT, MRCP

prompts.q: List the extra-intestinal manifestations of IBD.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: joints, eyes, skin, liver.

points.p: Crohn's: renal stones, B12 deficiency, fistulae

prompts.q: How is IBD investigated and confirmed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: screen, confirm, then stage.

points.why: Unprepared flexible sigmoidoscopy in severe flares.

points.p: AXR for toxic megacolon; MRI small bowel for Crohn's extent; MRI pelvis for perianal abscess
points.why: Pick the image by the question.

prompts.q: What separates UC and Crohn's on biopsy, and what is checked before drugs?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: granulomas versus crypt abscesses.

points.p: UC: crypt abscesses, goblet cell loss, mucosal only
Crohn's: transmural, non-caseating granulomas, more goblet cells
Chest X-ray before anti-TNF; hep B, C and HIV before immunosuppression

prompts.q: Outline the treatment ladder for UC, mild to severe.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: each step has a trigger to move up.

points.p: No response 48–72 h: IV ciclosporin plus surgical review; then colectomy
Maintenance: aminosalicylate, then azathioprine if ≥2 flares a year

prompts.q: How is Crohn's disease treated, and is surgery curative?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: steroids induce, thiopurines maintain.

points.p: Induction: oral prednisolone or budesonide; severe: IV hydrocortisone
Maintenance: azathioprine/mercaptopurine, then methotrexate, then biologics
Surgery not curative in Crohn's; colectomy curative in UC

prompts.q: Why do UC and Crohn's behave differently, and why does mesalazine suit UC?

points.p: UC mucosal and continuous; bleeds; toxic megacolon
Crohn's transmural with skip lesions; fistulae and strictures

glossary.IBD: Inflammatory bowel disease: ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease.
glossary.UC: Ulcerative colitis: continuous mucosal inflammation of the colon starting at the rectum.
glossary.IBS: Irritable bowel syndrome: functional bowel disorder with no inflammation or bleeding.
glossary.tenesmus: A constant feeling of needing to open the bowels even when empty.
glossary.skip lesions: Patches of inflamed bowel separated by normal bowel, typical of Crohn's.
glossary.cobblestone: Mucosa broken into raised islands by deep fissuring ulcers, typical of Crohn's.
glossary.transmural: Through the whole thickness of the bowel wall.
glossary.terminal ileum: Last part of the small intestine, where B12 and bile salts are absorbed.
glossary.pseudopolyps: Islands of regenerating mucosa between ulcers, seen in UC.
glossary.Truelove and Witts: Criteria grading UC flare severity by stool count and systemic markers.
glossary.toxic megacolon: Colon dilated over 6 cm with systemic toxicity; a surgical emergency.
glossary.PSC: Primary sclerosing cholangitis: fibrosing inflammation of bile ducts linked to UC.
glossary.primary sclerosing cholangitis: Chronic scarring of the bile ducts, linked to UC; diagnosed on MRCP.
glossary.cholangiocarcinoma: Cancer of the bile ducts; tumour marker CA 19-9.
glossary.MRCP: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography: MRI of the bile and pancreatic ducts.
glossary.ALP: Alkaline phosphatase: liver enzyme that rises most in bile duct obstruction or cholestasis.
glossary.erythema nodosum: Tender red nodules on the shins from inflamed fat.
glossary.pyoderma gangrenosum: Painful ulcer with a purple undermined edge, linked to IBD.
glossary.episcleritis: Mild, often painless redness of the eye surface; tracks IBD activity.
glossary.sacroiliitis: Inflammation of the sacroiliac joints causing low back pain.
glossary.fistula: Abnormal channel between two epithelial surfaces, such as bowel and bladder.
glossary.colovesical fistula: Fistula between colon and bladder; causes pneumaturia and recurrent UTIs.
glossary.seton: A loose thread placed through a fistula to keep it draining.
glossary.faecal calprotectin: Stool protein from neutrophils; raised in IBD, normal in IBS.
glossary.crypt abscesses: Neutrophils collecting in colonic crypts; a UC biopsy hallmark.
glossary.goblet cells: Mucus-secreting cells in the gut lining; lost in UC.
glossary.non-caseating granulomas: Clusters of macrophages without central necrosis; the Crohn's hallmark.
glossary.basal plasmacytosis: Plasma cells crowded at the base of the mucosa; a sign of chronic colitis.
glossary.TPMT: Thiopurine methyltransferase: enzyme breaking down azathioprine; low levels cause toxicity.
glossary.azathioprine: Thiopurine immunosuppressant for IBD maintenance; check TPMT first.
glossary.mercaptopurine: Thiopurine related to azathioprine, used for IBD maintenance.
glossary.mesalazine: 5-ASA aminosalicylate acting topically on colonic mucosa.
glossary.aminosalicylates: 5-ASA drugs such as mesalazine and sulfasalazine.
glossary.sulfasalazine: Aminosalicylate prodrug releasing 5-ASA in the colon.
glossary.budesonide: Steroid with high first-pass liver metabolism, used for Crohn's induction.
glossary.hydrocortisone: Corticosteroid given IV for acute severe UC.
glossary.ciclosporin: Calcineurin inhibitor used IV as rescue in steroid-refractory UC.
glossary.calcineurin inhibitors: Ciclosporin and tacrolimus; block T-cell activation.
glossary.infliximab: Anti-TNF-alpha monoclonal antibody for refractory IBD.
glossary.anti-TNF: Biologic drugs neutralising tumour necrosis factor alpha.
glossary.Th1: T helper 1 cells driving cell-mediated inflammation and granulomas.
glossary.methotrexate: Folate antagonist used for Crohn's maintenance.
glossary.colectomy: Surgical removal of the colon; curative in UC.
glossary.ileostomy: Opening of the ileum onto the abdominal wall.
glossary.LMWH: Low molecular weight heparin, used to prevent VTE in IBD flares.
glossary.flexible sigmoidoscopy: Camera examination of the rectum and sigmoid colon.

technique.stem: A 22 year old woman has had diarrhoea 4 times a day for 3 months without blood. She has lost 6 kg and has recurrent mouth ulcers. She smokes 15 cigarettes a day. There is a tender mass in the right iliac fossa and a perianal skin tag.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis in chronic diarrhoea: decide IBD or not, then which type.

clues: mass in the right iliac fossa
steps.x: Weight loss and a mass mean organic disease. Non-bloody, terminal ileal mass, mouth ulcers, perianal disease and smoking.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Crohn's disease** of the terminal ileum.

elim: Malabsorption and mouth ulcers, but no RIF mass or perianal disease.
Weight loss and a mass are red flags; not IBS.
Can mimic, but needs TB risk and systemic symptoms.
Bloody, rectal; smoking protects against it.

steps.x: **B. Crohn's disease.** Rule: RIF mass + mouth ulcers + perianal disease + smoker = Crohn's.

technique.stem: A 30 year old man has had bloody diarrhoea with urgency for 8 weeks. He is well, with 3 stools a day. Faecal calprotectin is 620 µg/g (<50). Stool cultures are negative.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: It asks for the diagnostic test: the one that confirms.
Infection excluded; calprotectin high; he is stable, so full colonoscopy is safe.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Colonoscopy with biopsy** is the gold standard.

elim: For toxic megacolon in a sick patient.

steps.x: **C. Colonoscopy with biopsy.** Rule: stable + suspected IBD = colonoscopy and biopsy; severe flare = unprepared flexible sigmoidoscopy.

technique.stem: A 34 year old woman with ulcerative colitis has had 8 bloody stools a day for 4 days. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 110/68 mmHg. Haemoglobin is 98 g/L (115–165). Abdominal X-ray shows no colonic dilatation.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management: grade the severity first.
Six or more bloody stools plus fever, tachycardia and anaemia: **acute severe UC** (Truelove and Witts).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Admit for **IV hydrocortisone**.

elim: Rescue if no response in 48–72 hours.
If medical therapy fails, or perforation.

steps.x: **B. IV hydrocortisone.** Rule: severe UC = IV steroids first, rescue at 72 hours.

technique.stem: A 26 year old man with Crohn's disease of the terminal ileum is starting infliximab after failing azathioprine. A chest X-ray is done first to exclude tuberculosis.
technique.q: Which is the mechanism of action of infliximab?
o: Local inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis in colonic mucosa

steps.x: Drug mechanism: name the class.
An anti-TNF biologic; TB reactivates without TNF, hence the X-ray.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Infliximab **neutralises TNF-alpha**, which drives Th1 granulomatous inflammation.
**D. Neutralisation of TNF-alpha.** Rule: '-mab' plus TB screen = anti-TNF.

practice.stem: A 26 year old man has had bloody diarrhoea 5 times a day for 6 weeks, with urgency, tenesmus and mucus. He stopped smoking 2 months ago. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. Abdominal examination is normal. Stool cultures are negative.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Bloody diarrhoea with tenesmus and urgency starting after stopping smoking is classic UC. Crohn's is linked to smoking and is often non-bloody.

steps.x: Diagnosis in bloody chronic diarrhoea.
Rectal symptoms (tenesmus, urgency), bloody, chronic, recent smoking cessation, infection excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ulcerative colitis**.

elim: Acute; cultures negative and 6 weeks long.
Usually non-bloody; smoking is a risk, not protective.
Acute terminal ileitis mimicking appendicitis; cultures are negative and this is 6 weeks of rectal symptoms.

steps.x: **D. Ulcerative colitis.** Rule: blood + tenesmus + ex-smoker = UC.

practice.stem: A 19 year old woman has had non-bloody diarrhoea and colicky right lower abdominal pain for 4 months. She has lost 7 kg and has painful mouth ulcers. She smokes. There is a tender mass in the right iliac fossa.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A tender RIF mass with weight loss, mouth ulcers and non-bloody diarrhoea in a smoker is terminal ileal Crohn's.

steps.x: Diagnosis in chronic diarrhoea with a mass.

clues: mass in the right iliac fossa
steps.x: Chronic course, weight loss, oral ulcers and a terminal ileal mass.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Crohn's disease**.

elim: Acute history with fever, not 4 months.
Does not cause diarrhoea and mouth ulcers.

steps.x: **C. Crohn's disease.** Rule: RIF mass + mouth ulcers + weight loss = Crohn's.

practice.stem: A 38 year old man with ulcerative colitis has had 7 bloody stools a day for 3 days. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which best describes the severity of this flare?
practice.e: Truelove and Witts: 6 or more bloody stools plus temperature >37.8°C, pulse >90 bpm or ESR >30 mm/h is severe UC needing admission.

steps.x: Grade severity using Truelove and Witts.
Six or more bloody stools plus at least one of: temperature >37.8°C, pulse >90, Hb <105, ESR >30. He has fever, a pulse over 90 and an ESR over 30.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Severe** UC.

elim: Needs colonic dilatation >6 cm and toxicity.

steps.x: **E. Severe ulcerative colitis.** Rule: ≥6 bloody stools + one systemic sign = severe.

practice.stem: A 46 year old man with a 20 year history of ulcerative colitis has itching and fatigue. He is mildly jaundiced. There is no abdominal pain.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: ALP disproportionately raised compared with ALT in UC means primary sclerosing cholangitis, diagnosed on MRCP. PBC is not linked to IBD.

steps.x: Diagnosis of liver disease in a UC patient.
Cholestatic picture: ALP far higher than ALT, in long-standing UC.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Primary sclerosing cholangitis**; confirm with MRCP.

elim: Mainly raised ALT; no new drug is mentioned.
Middle-aged women, AMA positive; not linked to UC.
Young patients with neurological or psychiatric signs; hepatitic, low caeruloplasmin.

steps.x: **D. Primary sclerosing cholangitis.** Rule: UC + cholestatic LFTs = PSC.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman with ulcerative colitis has been on IV hydrocortisone for 2 days. Her abdomen is now distended and very tender. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 126 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. Abdominal X-ray shows a transverse colon diameter of 9 cm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Colonic dilatation above 6 cm with fever, tachycardia above 120, leucocytosis and hypotension in a UC flare is toxic megacolon.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a UC complication.
Colon over 6 cm, fever above 38°C, pulse above 120, anaemia/leucocytosis, hypotension, despite steroids.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Toxic megacolon**.

elim: Twisted bowel in elderly, constipated; coffee-bean sign.
Small bowel loops, vomiting; the colon here is dilated.

steps.x: **E. Toxic megacolon.** Rule: UC + colon >6 cm + toxic = toxic megacolon.

practice.stem: A 24 year old man has had abdominal pain, non-bloody diarrhoea and weight loss for 5 months. He has perianal fistulae. Colonoscopy is performed.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding at colonoscopy?
practice.e: Crohn's gives discontinuous skip lesions and a cobblestone appearance. Continuous inflammation from the rectum is UC.

steps.x: Finding on colonoscopy: name the disease first.
Perianal fistulae and non-bloody diarrhoea with weight loss: Crohn's.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Skip lesions and cobblestone** mucosa.
**E. Skip lesions with cobblestone mucosa.** Rule: Crohn's on scope = skip lesions + cobblestones.

practice.stem: A 23 year old woman has had diarrhoea, weight loss and right iliac fossa pain for 3 months. Faecal calprotectin is raised. Colonoscopy shows terminal ileal ulceration and biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas. Her team now wants to know the extent of her disease.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to assess the extent of her disease?
practice.e: MRI small bowel is the best way to evaluate the extent of Crohn's disease. Colonoscopy cannot reach most of the small bowel.

steps.x: Staging the extent, not diagnosis: diagnosis is already made.
Crohn's confirmed; small bowel beyond the scope's reach needs imaging.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MRI small bowel**.

elim: Colon, not small bowel; radiation in a young patient.
Cannot see most of the small bowel.

steps.x: **D. MRI small bowel.** Rule: stage Crohn's = MRI small bowel; perianal abscess = MRI pelvis.

practice.stem: A 31 year old man with Crohn's disease needs maintenance therapy after his second flare this year. The team plans to start azathioprine.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation before starting?
practice.e: TPMT activity is checked before azathioprine to avoid neutropenia. A chest X-ray is the check before anti-TNF agents.

steps.x: Pre-treatment check for a named drug.
Azathioprine is metabolised by TPMT.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Check **TPMT activity**; low TPMT causes neutropenia.

elim: For steroid bone protection, not azathioprine.

steps.x: **D. Thiopurine methyltransferase activity.** Rule: azathioprine = TPMT; infliximab = chest X-ray.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman has a flare of ulcerative colitis with 9 bloody stools a day. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. She is admitted.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Acute severe UC is treated first with IV corticosteroids. Ciclosporin is rescue therapy at 48–72 hours.

steps.x: Initial management of a severe flare.
Acute severe UC by Truelove and Witts.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV hydrocortisone**, with LMWH and fluids.

elim: Only if no response after 48–72 hours.

steps.x: **B. IV hydrocortisone.** Rule: severe UC = IV steroids.

practice.stem: A 25 year old man with acute severe ulcerative colitis has received IV hydrocortisone for 72 hours. He still has 8 bloody stools a day. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Abdominal X-ray shows no dilatation.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue IV hydrocortisone for 7 more days
practice.e: Failure to respond to IV steroids in 48–72 hours needs IV ciclosporin (or infliximab) with surgical review; colectomy if that fails.

steps.x: Next step after failed IV steroids.
No response by 72 hours, not dilated.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV ciclosporin plus surgical review** (infliximab if ciclosporin contraindicated).

elim: Delay raises perforation and death risk.

steps.x: **B. IV ciclosporin with surgical review.** Rule: 72 hours without response = rescue therapy + surgeons.

practice.stem: A 32 year old woman has rectal bleeding and urgency. She opens her bowels 3 times a day and is otherwise well. Sigmoidoscopy shows inflammation confined to the rectum, and biopsy confirms ulcerative proctitis.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Mild UC proctitis is induced with topical mesalazine, then oral 5-ASA added if needed. Budesonide is used in Crohn's.

steps.x: Initial management of mild distal UC.
Mild proctitis: 4 or fewer stools, well.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Topical (rectal) mesalazine**, adding oral 5-ASA if needed.
**D. Rectal mesalazine.** Rule: mild proctitis = topical mesalazine.

practice.stem: A 35 year old man with long-standing Crohn's disease develops pneumaturia and recurrent urinary tract infections with mixed bowel organisms.
practice.q: Which feature of Crohn's disease best explains this complication?
practice.e: Transmural inflammation in Crohn's lets ulcers track through the wall into the bladder, forming a colovesical fistula.

steps.x: Mechanism of a complication.
Air and bowel flora in the urine: a **colovesical fistula**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fistulae form because Crohn's inflammation is **transmural**.
**E. Transmural inflammation.** Rule: fistula and stricture = transmural (Crohn's).
